# APPENDIX A · Lens · Transformation Brand

The brand is a named thing that leads with the change it produces rather than with the person producing it. A program, a method, a promise. It could, in principle, outlive its founder.

This is the lens with the most room to build — and the most room to build something hollow. A named brand can be invented from nothing, which means nothing is stopping you from inventing something the coach can't actually deliver.

---

## What changes by phase

### Phase 0 · Intake

Standard both-paths intake, plus:

- **What already has a name?** The business, the program, the framework, the free thing. Where did each name come from and does the coach still like it?
- **Is the method real yet?** There's a large difference between a coach who has run something twenty times and one who has a landing page. Both can build a brand; only one can make a claim. Establish which, early and without judgment, because it determines what the brand is allowed to promise.
- **The delivery reality.** How does the transformation actually happen — 1:1, group, cohort, self-paced, hybrid? Over what span? The brand has to fit the delivery or Phase 6 will catch the mismatch and you'll be rebuilding.

### Phase 1 · The Enemy

This lens supports the sharpest enemies, because the brand is an idea rather than a person and ideas can pick fights people can't.

Lean into the **industrial complex** category. A transformation brand's most defensible position is usually "an entire industry is set up to keep you in the problem, and here's the mechanism." That's a claim a named brand can make and sustain.

Watch for one failure: an enemy so broad it's unfalsifiable. "Modern life," "hustle culture," "the system" — these feel like positions and aren't, because nobody disagrees and nothing follows from them. Push for an enemy with a business model. If you can't name who makes money when the problem persists, keep going.

### Phase 2 · The Archetype

This lens gets the most leverage from the extension test, because the archetype has to name a whole product system rather than just describe a person.

Extend the standard five to include:

> 6. **The method's name** — the thing the coach does, as a proper noun
> 7. **The phases or steps** — what the stages of the work are called
> 8. **The diagnostic** — what you call the moment of assessment

When an archetype produces all eight cleanly, you have a brand that can generate its own product line indefinitely. That's the whole payoff of this lens: one metaphor choice, and the naming problem is permanently solved.

**Guard against the archetype outrunning the delivery.** A brand can promise a mechanical, systematic, diagnostic process; if the actual sessions are warm, exploratory conversations, the client feels the gap in week two. Run the marketing voice and the delivery voice against each other before locking the archetype — this is the mismatch the stress test hunts for and it's cheaper to catch here.

### Phase 3 · The Expensive Problem and the Transformation

The core of this lens. Everything else is downstream.

Additions:

- **The transformation needs a duration.** A named transformation brand almost always implies a span — 90 days, 12 weeks, six months. Pick it from the actual work, not from what sounds good. Then check: does the promise fit inside it honestly?
- **What's the observable milestone at the midpoint?** A client who can't tell it's working by the halfway mark churns, regardless of whether it's working.
- **What is explicitly *not* included?** A named brand invites scope creep because the name implies completeness. Draw the line here, in writing, and it'll save the coach a year of unpaid labor.

### Phase 4 · The People

Standard, with heavier weighting on the **buying-readiness split**. A transformation brand can be discovered by strangers at scale, which means the audience will be much broader than the buyer pool. Be explicit and unsentimental:

- Whose attention is this brand built to capture?
- Whose money is it built to take?
- Are those the same people? *(Often not, and that's fine — but it has to be a decision. Build the voice for the one who spreads it; take money from the one who's ready.)*

Then name **the beachhead**: one persona, for the next two quarters, that everything points at. Four personas is a research finding, not a go-to-market plan.

### Phase 5 · The Voice

This lens carries the most vocabulary, so build the lexicon properly and treat it as the real deliverable.

Three layers, and keep them visibly separate:

1. **Proprietary terms** — from the archetype. These are the brand's own words and they should be used with consistency bordering on stubbornness. Repetition is what turns a coined term into an asset.
2. **Methodology terms, verbatim** — from whatever certifications and trainings the coach holds. Do not rename these to fit the metaphor. The temptation is strong and the cost is real: renaming severs the credibility line back to the source, and it makes the coach's own training illegible to anyone else in that world. A coach with three modalities has three sub-layers, and all three stay intact.
3. **Bridge vocabulary** — the audience's native language, borrowed to make the work land instantly. This is where the metaphor meets the market.

Also build **the manifesto**. A transformation brand needs one long-form piece that shows the voice at length — 600 to 1,000 words, no headers, no bullets, the argument made in full. It becomes the calibration document: when anyone is unsure whether a piece of copy fits, they read it back to back with the manifesto and listen for the difference. This single artifact does more to make a brand voice reproducible than any list of adjectives.

### Phase 6 · The Stress Test

Add these charges:

11. **Is the differentiation categorical or only aesthetic?** The most dangerous failure in this lens. A distinctive font, a strong palette, and a coined vocabulary can make a brand *feel* different while the underlying offer is identical to six others. Ask: if you stripped the words and the design, what's structurally different about what the client receives?
12. **Can the brand survive the founder's absence — and does anyone want it to?** If the answer is no, this might actually be a personal brand wearing a program's name. That's worth knowing before building a brand architecture that assumes separability.
13. **Does the promise fit the duration?** A 90-day name attached to a change that takes two years is a refund waiting to happen.
14. **Does the positioning self-destruct if it succeeds?** Some positions are built on scarcity, contrarianism, or being unknown, and stop working at scale. Test the brand at 100x its current size and see what breaks.
15. **What's the proof?** A named brand makes a specific claim, which invites the question of evidence. If there are no results yet, the brand should be built so it can make claims *later* without contradicting what it says now.

### Phase 7 · Assembly

The Bible gains one section:

**Part IX · Brand Architecture**
- The master brand and what sits under it — programs, tiers, the free thing, the diagnostic.
- The naming convention: how future products get named from inside the metaphor, so the coach can name the next three things without another branding exercise.
- What the brand may and may not claim at its current level of evidence, and what unlocks each next claim.
- The relationship between the founder and the brand: how much of the founder is in it now, and what the plan is if that changes.


---

# APPENDIX B · Lens · Personal Brand

The coach's own name is the brand. They are the product, the marketing, and the delivery.

This lens has one great advantage and one great danger, and they're the same fact: there's nothing between the coach and the audience.

**The advantage** — no translation loss. What they believe reaches the client directly, and coherence is nearly free.

**The danger** — with no external object to point at, the brand collapses into a résumé. Certifications, credentials, "I help leaders unlock their potential." A personal brand without an enemy is just a person listing their qualifications, and that is the single most common failure in this entire category.

Enemy-first isn't merely useful here. It's the only thing that turns a biography into a position.

---

## What changes by phase

### Phase 0 · Intake

Weight the self path heavily. In this lens, the coach's own history isn't background — it's the product's origin story and often its proof.

Add:

- **The credential pile.** Every certification, in the order collected, with the year and what they were hoping it would fix. *(The sequence is revealing. People collect certifications in the direction of an unanswered question, and the question is usually the brand.)*
- **The public trail.** Everything they've published — posts, newsletters, talks, podcast appearances. What got a reaction? What did they think would land and didn't?
- **The thing they're known for by accident.** Most personal-brand coaches have one post, one line, or one story that outperformed everything else and they usually resent it. Find it, because the market has already voted.

### Phase 1 · The Enemy

Two risks specific to this lens.

**First: the enemy becomes a person.** In a personal brand, "against" slides easily into "against someone" — a competitor, an ex-mentor, a guru with more followers. That reads as insecurity and it ages badly. Keep the enemy structural: an industry, a received wisdom, a false cure, a category. Heat is for systems, not people.

**Second: no enemy at all.** Coaches who are conflict-averse, or who trained in modalities that prize neutrality, will resist this phase. Don't let them skip it. Reframe: *you're not attacking anyone, you're being specific about what this isn't — and that specificity is what lets the right person recognize themselves.* The kindest thing a brand can do is be legible enough that the wrong people can leave.

### Phase 2 · The Archetype

The archetype is the coach's own working self, so the elicitation is closer and the honesty bar is higher.

The trap: choosing the archetype they wish they were. A quiet, patient coach who selects a provocateur archetype because it markets well will produce excellent copy and then dread every post. This is exactly what the Vocational-Fit Check exists to catch, and in this lens it is the highest-stakes check in the kit.

Ask directly:

- Who are you on your *best* day with a client — not your most impressive day?
- What do people thank you for afterward? Is it the same thing you think you're good at?
- Is there a version of you that shows up when you're tired, and is it recognizably the same person as the one in this brand?

The last one matters more than it sounds. A personal brand has to hold up on a bad week, because there's no institution to hide behind.

Also handle: **the name.** If the coach's own name is the brand, the archetype has to be expressible *through* a name they didn't choose. That's a constraint, not a problem — it just means the archetype lives in the vocabulary and the visual system rather than in a clever wordmark. Consider whether a named *method* or *program* should carry the metaphor instead, so the archetype has somewhere concrete to live.

### Phase 3 · The Expensive Problem and the Transformation

Standard, with one addition: **check the proximity trap.** Personal-brand coaches frequently define the expensive problem as the one *they* had, which is legitimate — being the former patient is real authority — but it can quietly narrow the market to "people exactly like me at 34."

Ask:

- Is this problem specific to your story, or do you see it in people whose lives look nothing like yours?
- If someone had this problem for completely different reasons, would your work still help them?

The answer changes the size of the business. Either answer is fine. Not knowing which one is true is not.

### Phase 4 · The People

Add: **the parasocial layer.** In a personal brand, a meaningful portion of the audience is there for the coach, not the transformation. That's an asset and a liability. Get explicit about it:

- Who follows you and will never buy? What are they getting?
- What do you want from an audience — clients, or reach that turns into something else later?
- Is there a version of this where you're famous and broke?

### Phase 5 · The Voice

Easier here, because the voice already exists — it's how they talk. The work is capture, not invention.

Best move: **pull from unpolished sources.** Voice memos, DMs, a text to a friend explaining what they do, the transcript of a session, a rant. The website voice is the one they don't like. The friend voice is the brand.

Registers still apply, but the private-to-public distance should be *short*. If the coaching-room voice and the content voice sound like different people, the audience will feel the switch on the first call and it reads as a bait-and-switch.

### Phase 6 · The Stress Test

Add these charges:

11. **What happens when they're sick, on holiday, or done?** A personal brand has no bus factor. Name it honestly: is this a business or a job? Both are fine; only one of them can be sold.
12. **Is the brand a burnout script?** Particularly acute here — the coach is the entire supply. If the identity requires constant visibility, constant sharpness, constant output, it will eat them. Ask what this brand looks like at 60% capacity, because there will be months at 60%.
13. **Is the public self sustainable?** A performed identity is exhausting in a way a designed one isn't. If the answer to "who are you on a bad week" doesn't match the brand, revise the brand rather than the person.
14. **Does the credential stack support or undermine the position?** Fourteen certifications listed on an about page signal searching, not authority. Decide which two or three earn their place publicly; the rest work quietly inside the method.

### Phase 7 · Assembly

The Bible gains one section:

**Part IX · The Operator**
- The bio, in three lengths: one line, one paragraph, one page.
- The origin story, told as the coach's hero journey against the enemy — not as a CV.
- What they're publicly credentialed in and what they use quietly.
- Sustainability terms: what this brand requires weekly, and what it looks like at reduced capacity.
- The succession question, answered honestly: is there a version of this that runs without them, and do they want one?


---

# APPENDIX C · Lens · Brick-and-Mortar

Gyms, studios, clinics, boxes, dojos, practices. Anywhere with a front door, a room, and other people delivering the work.

This is the lens that bends the spine hardest, because a physical coaching business has **three audiences, not one**, and the usual brand kit only knows about one of them.

---

## The three audiences

| Audience | What they need from the brand |
|---|---|
| **The member** | A reason to walk in and a reason to stay. |
| **The staff** | An identity they can carry on the floor without being told what to say each time. |
| **The owner** | A vision clear enough to lead from — including the ability to hire, train, and let go against it. |

The owner audience is the one everybody forgets. A brick-and-mortar owner in an identity crisis is usually not confused about marketing. They're confused about **what they want this place to be**, and every marketing problem downstream is a symptom of that.

So for this lens, the Brand Bible is not a marketing document. It's a **leadership document that happens to include marketing.** Write it so the owner reads it and knows how to run the room — and so a coach on the floor reads it and knows what this place believes.

**Do not produce a separate one-page "floor card" or staff summary.** Splitting it invites a two-tier brand where the owner has the real vision and the staff get a laminated abbreviation of it. The Bible itself carries both jobs.

---

## What changes by phase

### Phase 0 · Intake

Add to the standard intake:

- **The room itself.** What does it smell like, sound like, look like at 6am versus 6pm? What's on the walls? What did the last owner leave behind that's still there?
- **The staff.** How many coaches, how long have they been there, where did they come from, what do they believe? Are they employees, contractors, or former members who got certified?
- **Membership shape.** How many members, how long do they stay, when do they leave? Churn by month of tenure if they have it. *(Churn at month 3 is an onboarding problem. Churn at month 14 is an identity problem — the place never became theirs.)*
- **Local reality.** Who else is within fifteen minutes, what do they charge, what do they call themselves? A physical business competes with geography, not with a niche.
- **The failed pivots — in detail.** Physical businesses pivot by buying a licensed program or methodology, and those pivots leave marks: members who left, staff who disagreed, equipment in a corner. Ask what they bought, what it promised, why they bought it, and what actually happened. This is usually the richest material in the entire intake.

### Phase 1 · The Enemy

The adjacent-category antagonist does most of the work here and it's usually one of these shapes:

- The commodity version of what they do (the $10 gym, the chain studio, the mill practice).
- The elite version that excludes their people (the competitive box, the boutique that's really a fashion brand).
- The methodology they used to belong to and outgrew.
- The industry's own churn model — businesses that make money on members who never come.

Push past "we're more welcoming." Every gym in America says it's welcoming. Ask what they're *against*, not what they're nicer than.

**A note on outgrown affiliations.** Many owners bought into a methodology, gave it years, and drifted. There's grief in that and it comes out as vagueness. Name it directly: *what did that thing give you that was real, and what did it stop giving you?* The honest answer usually contains the enemy — not the methodology itself, but the thing it turned into.

### Phase 2 · The Archetype

Two archetypes exist here and they must be separated or the brand will be incoherent the moment the owner steps off the floor.

1. **The owner's archetype** — how *they* coach and lead.
2. **The place's archetype** — what the room is, which has to survive the owner not being in it.

A personal-brand coach can collapse these. A brick-and-mortar owner cannot, because they're building something staff have to deliver. Ask: *if you were on vacation for three weeks, what would still be true about this place?* That's the place's archetype. Anything that evaporates was yours, not the building's.

The extension test applies to the place's archetype and gains two items:

> From inside this metaphor, name:
> 1. The membership tiers or programs
> 2. The first free thing (a drop-in, a trial, an assessment)
> 3. The verb on the button
> 4. What you call someone who's stuck
> 5. What you call it when it works
> 6. **What you call your members collectively**
> 7. **What you call the room, or the parts of it**

### Phase 3 · The Expensive Problem and the Transformation

Harder here, because members don't arrive with a crisp problem — they arrive with a body, a schedule, and a vague intention. The expensive problem is real but it's usually *ahead* of them rather than behind.

Useful reframes:

- What are these people going to lose in the next ten years if nothing changes? Be concrete — independence, a knee, being able to pick up a grandchild, a decade of energy.
- What did the ones who stayed five years get that the ones who quit at month four didn't?
- What's the thing members say at year two that they'd never have said at week one? *(That sentence is usually the actual transformation.)*

**The retention insight belongs here, not in marketing.** For a physical business, the money is in the difference between a nine-month member and a four-year member. So the transformation you name should be the one that takes years, not the one that takes six weeks — because the six-week promise is what every competitor is already making, and it's also what produces churn at month nine when the six weeks are over and there's nothing after it.

### Phase 4 · The People

Two additions:

- **Segment by tenure as well as by failure mode.** The person walking in the door and the person four years in are different people with different reasons to be there, and a brand that only speaks to the first one leaks its best members.
- **Add a staff persona.** Who is the coach you want on the floor? What do they believe, what did they do before, why would they work here instead of somewhere paying more? You are recruiting against this, and a place whose identity attracts the right coaches has solved half of its delivery problem.

Also: the local constraint. A niche-by-psychographic (the burned-out senior engineer) works for an online transformation brand. A physical business needs a position sharp enough to be distinctive but broad enough that enough of those people live within fifteen minutes. Say the tradeoff out loud and make the owner choose it deliberately.

### Phase 5 · The Voice

Add a fourth register: **the floor voice.** How a coach talks to a member mid-workout, mid-session, mid-appointment. It's the register the brand actually lives or dies in, and it's the one no brand guide ever documents.

For the floor voice, capture:

- What we say when someone shows up after three weeks away. *(This one sentence tells you more about a gym's real culture than its entire website.)*
- What we say when someone scales down, modifies, or can't finish.
- What we say when someone hits something they've been chasing.
- What we say to a first-timer in the first ninety seconds.
- What we never say. Especially: the sarcastic thing, the comparison to another member, the joke about how hard it's going to be.

The methodology layer matters here too — the technical vocabulary of whatever the staff are certified in stays verbatim, because that's what makes the coaching sound like coaching rather than customer service.

### Phase 6 · The Stress Test

Add these charges to the standard ten:

11. **Can a 24-year-old coach two months into the job deliver this identity on the floor without being coached on it every shift?** If it only works when the owner is in the building, it isn't an identity, it's a personality.
12. **Would you fire someone over this?** An owner who won't let a coach go for violating the values doesn't have values, they have preferences. Name the specific behavior that would end an employment.
13. **Does the room match?** Walk the space against the brand you just wrote. The walls, the music, the whiteboard, the front desk, the bathroom. Physical space is the highest-bandwidth brand surface a business can have and it's usually the last one anyone audits.
14. **Does this survive the local market?** Are there enough of these people within a reasonable drive at this price?
15. **Does the owner want to run this business, or the one they had five years ago?** Grief for the old version masquerades as strategy more often in this lens than in either of the others.

### Phase 7 · Assembly

The Bible gains two sections and one has to be written for a reader who is not the owner.

**Part IX · Leading This Place** *(for the owner)*
- What we believe, in a form the owner can lead from.
- The three or four values, each written as an observable behavior rather than a word. Not "community" — *we know every member's name inside two visits and we say it when they walk in.*
- What gets someone hired here. What gets someone let go.
- What the owner personally owns and what belongs to the staff.
- The one-year vision for the room: what's different in twelve months, described physically.

**Part X · Working Here** *(for the staff)*
- Who we are and who we're against, in plain language, no marketing register.
- What we say and don't say on the floor.
- What a member should feel in their first ninety seconds, at week six, and at year two.
- The three sentences that explain this place to someone who asks at a party.

Write Part X so a coach could read it once, hand it back, and be right. If it requires the owner's presence to interpret, rewrite it.

---

## Grounding note

The real case this lens was built against: an owner with a decade of coaching and seven years of ownership, who took over a box he'd worked at, carried it through COVID, and lost the community spark it had originally. He tried adopting a licensed methodology and it went badly. He tried going back to the roots and it felt empty. He can't articulate the values, doesn't see a strong identity in the business, and has no picture of what he wants it to deliver — for members *or* for his coaching staff.

Two things that case teaches about this lens:

**The two failed pivots are the most valuable intake material available.** One was reaching forward for an identity, one was reaching backward. Both failed, which means the answer isn't in either direction — and knowing that eliminates most of the search space before you ask a single identity question.

**"Lost the community spark" is not a marketing problem.** It's an owner who no longer knows what the room is for. Do not let this lens drift into logos and Instagram. The deliverable is a leader who knows what he's building and a staff who can say it out loud.


---

# APPENDIX D · Question Bank

The actual questions. Ask them in plain language, one at a time in Phases 0–3.

These are written the way you should say them. Resist the urge to make them more professional — a coach answers a blunt question honestly and a polished question with marketing copy.

**Contents**

- [How to ask](#how-to-ask)
- [Phase 0 · Intake](#phase-0--intake)
- [Phase 1 · The Enemy](#phase-1--the-enemy)
- [Phase 2 · The Archetype](#phase-2--the-archetype)
- [Phase 3 · The Expensive Problem and the Transformation](#phase-3--the-expensive-problem-and-the-transformation)
- [Phase 4 · The People](#phase-4--the-people)
- [Phase 5 · The Voice](#phase-5--the-voice)
- [Follow-up moves that work on any answer](#follow-up-moves-that-work-on-any-answer)

---

## How to ask

**One at a time in Phases 0–3.** Six questions at once gets you the three easy answers and silence on the one that mattered.

**Let them ramble, then reflect back the sharpest fragment.** Coaches think out loud. The usable material is almost never the summary they give at the end — it's the aside in the middle, the thing they said quickly because they assumed it was obvious. When you hear it, quote it back verbatim and ask if that's the real answer.

**Prefer their words to yours.** If a coach says "people show up already apologizing," never upgrade that to "clients present with anticipatory deference." You just deleted the brand.

**When an answer is abstract, ask for the last specific time it happened.** Abstraction is where the generic lives. A story has details you can build with.

---

## Phase 0 · Intake

### The history path — ask everyone, regardless of tenure

- How long have you been doing this, and how many people have you worked with — roughly?
- Tell me about one client or member you were unusually good for. What was going on with them when they arrived?
- Now tell me about one you couldn't help. What happened?
- When someone quits or doesn't renew, what reason do they give? And what do you think the real reason is?
- What do people say to you at the door, or in the first five minutes of a first call? Same words, over and over — what are they?
- If you have testimonials or reviews, paste them in. Don't clean them up. The typos are data.
- What do your staff or peers hear from clients that you don't?

### The failed attempts — spend real time here

Failures name the enemy faster than successes do, because they mark where you tried to be something the market refused.

- What have you tried in the last few years that didn't work? A program, a pivot, a marketing push, a positioning?
- Walk me through one of those. What did you hope would happen, and what actually happened?
- How did it feel to be doing that work? Not whether it made money — whether you wanted to keep doing it.
- Is there something you *used* to do that you quietly stopped, and never announced?

### The self path — ask everyone, including ten-year veterans

- What were you doing for a living before this?
- Were you ever the person you now work with? What happened to you?
- What do people ask you about at parties, once they find out what you do?
- What do you find yourself ranting about? To your partner, to a friend, in your head at 2am?
- What's the thing you believe about this work that would get you in trouble with your peers?

### The toolkit

- List every certification, training, and method you use with clients — all of them, in the order you actually reach for them in a session.
- Which one do you lead with when you describe what you do? Which ones do you use but never mention?
- Are there terms from those trainings you'd never want changed or reworded?

### The existing assets

- What's the business called right now, and where did that name come from?
- What are your programs or services called?
- Send me your website, your Instagram bio, your LinkedIn headline — whatever's public.
- On a scale of "carved in stone" to "burn it down," how attached are you to the current name?

*(Ask the attachment question regardless of the answer you expect. The Contradiction Check still runs either way — knowing where they stand just changes how you deliver it.)*

---

## Phase 1 · The Enemy

Open here. It works on almost everyone:

> **What's the lie in your industry?**

Then follow the heat. Below are prompts for each of the four categories if they stall.

### The industrial complex

- Who makes money when your clients stay stuck?
- What's an entire industry built on a problem never getting solved?
- What do people spend money on for years without getting better?
- Whose business model requires your client's problem to be permanent and complicated?

### The received wisdom

- What's the standard advice in your field that you think is wrong?
- What does every peer of yours say that makes you wince?
- What's true but useless? (Often more interesting than what's false.)
- If you gave a talk at your industry's conference and told the truth, what would make the room go quiet?

### The adjacent category

- What do people assume you are, that you're not?
- Who gets confused with you, that you want nothing to do with?
- Finish this: "People think this is ___, but it isn't."
- What's the compliment you hate receiving?

### The false cure

This one doubles as market research — a client's failed purchases are a map of the whole category.

- What has your client already bought that didn't fix this? List everything.
- What did they think that thing was going to do?
- Why didn't it work — mechanically, not emotionally?
- What do they say about it now? ("I did therapy for three years and—")

### Ranking and pressure-testing

- Of everything you just said, which one would you argue about at a dinner party, unprompted, with someone you'd just met?
- Now make the best case *for* the thing you're against. Seriously — the strongest honest version.
  - *(If they can't, they don't understand it well enough to attack it, and the audience will hear that. Work on this until they can.)*
- Is there anyone you're against that you're actually just jealous of? Worth knowing before it ends up in the copy.

### Then run the Inversion Pass

Give them: the obvious enemy, the genuine inverse, and a third framing that moves the problem into a different category. Ask which one makes them lean forward.

---

## Phase 2 · The Archetype

Elicit from history, not aspiration. The archetype has to be something they already are on a good day.

### Where they came from

- What did you do before this, and what did you get good at there?
- What skill from that life do you still use every day in this one?
- What did people rely on you for, before you were a coach?

### How they actually work

- Think of a session that went really well. What were you doing — with your hands, your voice, your body? Were you sitting? Moving? Writing?
- What do you do that other coaches in your space don't do?
- What do you flatly refuse to do that most of them do?
- When a client is upset, what's your instinct? Move toward it, name it, redirect it, sit in it?
- Are you more useful in the first ten minutes or the last ten?

### What people already call them

- What do people come to you for that isn't coaching?
- Has anyone ever described you in a way that stuck? What did they say?
- What's your nickname, if you have one? Who gave it to you?

### The extension test

Once you have candidates, run this out loud. It's the difference between an archetype and a decoration.

> From inside this metaphor, name:
> 1. The product
> 2. The first free thing someone gets
> 3. The verb on the button
> 4. What it's called when someone is stuck
> 5. What it's called when it works

If four of five come easily, it's a system — keep it. If you're straining, it's decoration — take the next candidate.

### The two hero journeys

- Tell me your version of this story: what were you like before you understood this, what happened, and what are you now?
- Now the same story for your client. Same enemy, different rank.

### Vocational-Fit Check

- Could you make this argument, in this voice, every week for a year — and still want to?
- Is this who you actually are on a good day, or who you'd like to be?
- Reading this back: does it make you want to go post something right now, or does it make you tired?

---

## Phase 3 · The Expensive Problem and the Transformation

**The stuck phase. Go slow. Do not accept the first answer, or the second.**

### The expensive problem

Open:

> **What expensive problem do you solve, and for exactly whom?**

Then the drill. Ask "and what does that cost them?" repeatedly until the answer contains a number, a relationship, or a span of years.

- What does this problem cost them in money? Be specific — a promotion, a season, a client roster, a business.
- What does it cost them in relationships? Who else is paying for this?
- How long have they had it? What did it cost them last year that they haven't counted?
- What's the thing they'd be doing right now if this weren't happening?
- What do they lose that they can't get back?

**Reject these answers:** stress, overwhelm, not living up to potential, lack of confidence, feeling stuck. They're symptoms, they're free, and everyone claims them. Keep going.

**Accept answers like:** a marriage, a body they can't get back after 50, a promotion that went to someone else, a business that stayed at $400K for six years, a decade in a career they chose at 22.

### The transformation

Open:

> **Describe what someone looks like before, and what they look like after — from the outside. What would a stranger watching notice?**

- What can they do after that they couldn't do before? A specific action.
- What do they stop doing?
- What's the first thing that changes — the earliest visible sign it's working?
- What does someone in their life say about them, three months in?
- If I filmed them before and after, what's in the two clips?

**If the change is purely internal, keep digging.** Internal shifts always have external tells, and the tell is the thing you can actually sell. "More confident" becomes "asks for the number without apologizing first." "Less anxious" becomes "eats lunch away from their desk." "More self-worth" becomes "left the gym at 6 instead of staying until 9."

### Cost of inaction

- If they do nothing and we talk in two years, where are they?
- What's the version of this that ends badly? How does it actually end?
- Is there a deadline built into their situation — an age, a contract, a body, a kid getting older, a business running out of runway?

### Price sanity

- What are you charging now, and how did you land on that?
- Against everything we just listed as the cost of inaction, is that number ridiculous in either direction?
- What would you have to believe about yourself to charge triple?
- Who else in the market charges what for what, and what do they actually deliver?

*(If the price is a small fraction of the cost of inaction and it still feels expensive to say out loud, the problem is the articulation of the cost, not the price. Fix the articulation.)*

### Gate A

Before moving on, run the Vocational-Fit Check again and a short adversarial pass:

- Say your positioning in one sentence, out loud, as if to a stranger at a party.
- Who would hear that and immediately not be your client? (If nobody, it's too broad.)
- What's the strongest argument that you're wrong about this problem?
- Is anyone already solving this well? What would they say about your version?

---

## Phase 4 · The People

Batching is fine from here on.

### Deriving the failure modes

- Think about everyone you've worked with on this problem. Does it show up the same way in all of them, or are there different flavors?
- Sort them: what are the two to four *characteristic* ways this goes wrong in different people?
- For each one, what's the sentence that person says to themselves? (Not what they say to you — what runs underneath.)

### Per persona

- Name them. Give me an age, a job, a life situation.
- What do they say out loud on a first call?
- What do they say to their partner at 11pm?
- What are they thinking in the parking lot before they walk in?
- What do they say when they cancel?
- **What have they already spent money on for this?** List everything — apps, programs, therapists, courses, equipment, retreats, supplements, another gym.
- Looking at that list: what kind of thing do they buy? Are they buying amplifiers, escape routes, vibes, systems, or permission? *(What they buy reveals what they think is wrong with them — which is usually the misdiagnosis you're correcting.)*
- What compliment do they not notice you paying them?
- What's the thing you could say that would make them feel seen and slightly caught?

### Buying readiness — ranked separately from pain

Ask explicitly, because these come apart and conflating them builds businesses around people who never purchase.

- Which of these people has actually paid you? Which ones almost did?
- Who has the money and the permission to spend it on themselves? (Those are two different things and the second one is usually the constraint.)
- Who reads everything you post for a year and never buys?
- Who, when they buy, brings other people with them?
- If you could only serve one for the next six months, which one — and is that the same as the one you find most interesting?

*(Building the voice for one persona while taking money from another is a legitimate strategy. It just has to be a decision rather than an accident.)*

### Objections

- What are the five things people say when they don't buy?
- For each: what's the belief underneath it? What is that objection defending?

*(Every objection is the persona's script defending itself. The response isn't to argue — it's to name it back.)*

### Grounding

Use web search to find how these people actually talk in public — forums, reviews, subreddits, comments under competitors' content, job posts if it's work-related. Bring back real sentences. Synthesis plus real language beats either alone.

**Then flag it:** these personas are hypotheses until real humans have been interviewed. Phase 6 assigns that.

---

## Phase 5 · The Voice

### The NO list

- What words in your industry make you cringe?
- What phrase, if it appeared on your website, would mean something had gone wrong?
- What do your *clients* say that you'd never repeat back to them? *(These are the tempting ones — a coach mirrors client language by reflex.)*
- What's the compliment that means you've drifted?

For each banned word, write one line on why. The reason is what makes the rule survive a contractor who doesn't share the coach's taste.

### The YES list

- What terms are yours — that you made up, or use in a specific way nobody else does?
- From your certifications and trainings: which terms do you keep exactly as taught, and why? *(Fidelity here is credibility. Don't let anyone rename these.)*
- What words from your audience's own world can you borrow to make this land instantly?

### Registers

- How do you sound when you're trying to stop a stranger from scrolling past?
- How do you sound on a sales call with someone who's nervous about the money?
- How do you sound in the room, with a client, when nobody's watching?

*(Same voice, three volumes. If they're three different people, that's a bait-and-switch and Phase 6 will catch it.)*

### Anti-patterns

- Send me three things you've written that you *almost* liked. Not the bad ones — the near-misses.

Near-misses teach far more than obvious failures, because the failure is subtle and nameable. For each: show the original, name the specific axis it failed on, rewrite it.

### The gut check

Build five yes/no questions any piece of copy has to pass, derived from what *this* brand keeps getting wrong. Not a template — a specific set of tripwires for their specific drift.

---

## Follow-up moves that work on any answer

- **"When was the last time that happened? Walk me through it."** Converts abstraction into a story with usable detail.
- **"Say that again, shorter."** Coaches over-explain. The third version is usually the line.
- **"You said [exact quote]. Is that the real answer?"** Reflecting a verbatim fragment is the single highest-yield move in the whole kit.
- **"What would you say if you weren't worried about sounding arrogant?"** Removes the hedge that's flattening the answer.
- **"Who would be annoyed by that?"** If nobody, it's too safe to be a position.
- **"What's the version of that you'd only say to a friend?"** That's the brand voice. The other one is the website voice they already have and don't like.


---

# APPENDIX E · The Stress Test

Phase 6. Two halves — an adversarial review, then falsifiable homework. Both are required.

The reason this phase exists: everything up to now has been a conversation between a coach and a machine that is structurally inclined to agree with them. The coach is going to feel great. Feeling great is not evidence, and the worst outcome this kit can produce is a beautifully coherent brand that the market has never been asked about.

---

## Half A · The Hard Cuts

### How to run it

Deliver the cuts **one at a time**, not as a list. A list gets skimmed and the coach accepts the easy ones. One at a time, each gets a real answer.

For each cut: state the charge, show the specific evidence from what you've built together, and ask for a verdict — **accept, reject, or defer.**

Then honor the verdict. A rejected cut is information: it tells you what the coach actually believes and won't be talked out of, and that conviction is usually load-bearing. Record rejections in the Bible. Don't relitigate.

**Do not soften a cut because the coach is excited.** Their excitement is the thing you're testing. If a charge is real, say it plainly and let them decide.

**Tone:** you are on their side. This is not a takedown — it's the last cheap chance to find the flaw. Frame it that way and coaches engage with it rather than defending.

---

### The standing charges

Run all ten. Add the lens-specific charges from the relevant lens file.

**1 · Aesthetic differentiation masquerading as categorical differentiation.**
A distinctive palette, a coined vocabulary, and a strong voice can make an ordinary offer feel novel. Strip the words and the design: what is structurally different about what this client receives, compared to the three closest alternatives? If the answer is "the feel of it," that's a real advantage but a fragile one, and the coach should know which they've got.

**2 · Marketing voice versus delivery voice.**
Read a piece of the content voice and a piece of the in-session voice back to back. Would a client meeting both feel misled? A combative brand attached to a gentle program produces refunds in week two. Either the delivery gets sharper or the marketing gets honest — but they have to agree.

**3 · Too many personas.**
Which single one is the beachhead for the next two quarters? Four personas is a research finding; it is not a plan. If the coach can't pick, ask which one has already paid them, and start there.

**4 · Price without proof.**
What evidence supports this number? Conviction is not evidence. If there are no results yet, that's fine — but the pricing story needs to be about the cost of inaction and the access being purchased, not about outcomes that haven't happened. Also check the reverse: a price far below the value described is its own credibility problem.

**5 · Positioning that self-destructs on success.**
Some positions depend on being the outsider, the small one, the one nobody's heard of, or the one attacking the establishment. Run the brand at a hundred times its current size and see what breaks. If success makes the coach into the thing they're against, revise now.

**6 · Scope, safety, and the person in crisis.**
Someone is going to arrive who needs more than coaching. What happens? This is not paperwork — it's the exposure that ends coaching businesses and hurts people. Required: a screening question, a referral list, a clear scope statement, and a rule for what the coach does when they see something clinical. Any brand that trades in psychological language needs this before it takes money.

**7 · The brand as a burnout script for the coach.**
Especially, but not only, when the brand is *about* burnout. Does this identity require constant output, constant sharpness, constant visibility? What does it look like at 60% capacity? If there's no answer, the coach has designed a job they'll quit.

**8 · Collision with existing obligations.**
Day job, non-compete, current clients, a partner's expectations, a landlord, a licensing body. Does anything here create a conflict the coach hasn't looked at directly? Ask about the day job specifically — it's the most commonly avoided answer in the whole phase.

**9 · Machinery before humans.**
Is the coach about to build a funnel, an email sequence, a course platform, and a booking system before a single person has paid them for this? Sequence it: sell to five people by hand first. Automation of a thing that doesn't convert just makes the failure faster and more expensive.

**10 · Unresolved contradictions.**
Every collision the Contradiction Check surfaced along the way, gathered and stated once more together. Existing name versus new positioning. Program names versus the archetype. Public bio versus the identity. The coach can keep all of it — but it goes in the Bible as a known, chosen contradiction rather than an accident.

---

### After the cuts

Revise whatever the coach accepted, then run the **Vocational-Fit Check** one final time on the revised version:

- Could you make this argument, in this voice, every week for a year — and still want to?
- Is this pointed at what you're actually good at?
- Reading it now, after all that: does it make you want to go post something, or does it make you tired?

If the energy dropped during the cuts, find out where. Sometimes a cut removed something that was doing real work and it needs restoring in a different form. Sometimes the drop reveals the coach was in love with a version of themselves rather than the work, which is worth knowing before they spend a year on it.

---

## Half B · The Field Test

The homework. Without it, everything above is a hall of mirrors.

### The assignment, as you should give it to the coach

> Find five real people in your network who fit your primary persona. Not clients — people. A former colleague, a friend of a friend, someone in a group you're in.
>
> Ask each of them for thirty minutes. Tell them the truth: you're doing research and you want to understand their experience, not sell them anything. **Do not pitch. Do not describe your brand.** The moment they know what you want to hear, the data is gone.
>
> Ask about their experience of the problem: when it started, what they've tried, what it's cost them, what they've spent money on, what they'd say to someone else in it.
>
> Record them, with permission. Bring the recordings back.

### Why the no-pitch rule is absolute

The coach has just spent hours building a beautiful description of this person's inner life. They will be desperate to test it, and testing it by describing it is how you get a false positive — people agree with confident descriptions of themselves, especially from someone they like.

The only useful signal is unprompted language: whether they reach for the same words the personas use, whether the expensive problem shows up in their account of their own life without being suggested, and whether the false cures on the persona's spend list appear on theirs.

### Interview questions to hand the coach

- Tell me about the last time [the problem] really got in the way. What happened?
- How long has this been going on?
- What have you tried? Walk me through each one.
- What did you think each of those was going to do? What actually happened?
- What has this cost you? *(Then stay quiet. The silence does the work.)*
- If nothing changes in two years, where are you?
- What would have to be true for you to spend real money solving this?
- Who else do you know dealing with the same thing?

### What to do with the recordings

Hand off to the **Persona Validation** skill. It compares real language against the drafted personas and reports where they hold, where they drift, and where the coach invented something that doesn't exist.

Until that's done, mark the personas in the Bible as **UNVALIDATED** in plain sight. A coach who forgets which parts are hypotheses will build a year of content on a person who isn't real.

---

## What good looks like coming out of this phase

- Three to six cuts accepted and the brand revised for them.
- One or two cuts rejected, with the coach's reasoning recorded.
- A named beachhead persona.
- A scope-and-referral answer that exists in writing.
- Five names on a list, with the field-test assignment scheduled.
- The coach still wanting to do it. If that's gone, something upstream is wrong and it's worth going back rather than shipping a Bible into a shrug.


---

# APPENDIX F · The Brand Bible Template

Phase 7. Assemble everything into one working document.

**Write it as a tool, not a trophy.** The test: could a contractor, a copywriter, a new staff member, or an AI tool be handed this document with no other context and produce something on-brand? Every section should be usable by someone who wasn't in the room.

**Keep the coach's own words wherever possible.** If the Bible reads better than anything the coach has ever said, you've overwritten them, and they will quietly stop using it. Their phrasing, sharpened — not your phrasing, imposed.

**Show, don't characterize.** "The voice is bold and direct" tells a writer nothing. Three example lines and three counter-examples tell them everything. Every voice claim in this document should be followed by evidence.

---

## Structure

Adjust part numbering to fit; the lens adds Part IX (and Part X for brick-and-mortar).

```
COVER — brand name, version, date, operator, intended use
PART I    · The Foundation
PART II   · The Persona
PART III  · Voice
PART IV   · Lexicon
PART V    · Persona Hooks
PART VI   · The Copy Engine
PART VII  · Visual Identity  [stub → Production Kit skill]
PART VIII · The Quality Bar
PART IX   · [lens-specific]
PART X    · [brick-and-mortar only: Working Here]
COLOPHON  — sources, version history, known contradictions
```

---

## Cover

Brand name. Version number (start at 1.0). Date. Who operates it. One line on what the document is for and who should read it.

Include one sentence naming what this document is the source of truth *for* — landing page copy, content, designer briefs, staff onboarding, AI tools. It tells a reader whether they're in the right place.

---

## PART I · The Foundation

**1.1 The Flag** — one paragraph: what this brand is against, and what it's the antidote to. Name the enemy explicitly. This paragraph is the reason the rest of the document is different from every other brand guide, so it goes first.

**1.2 Positioning statement** — one paragraph in this shape: *For [specific person] who [specific expensive situation], [brand] is [what it is]. Unlike [alternative], which [what it does wrong], we [what we do instead].*

**1.3 The operating verbs** *(if the archetype produced them)* — two or three verbs that name what the brand does, defined so they can't be used interchangeably. A brand with two well-defined verbs can describe its whole funnel in four words.

**1.4 The promise** — what a client will have at the end, stated concretely enough to be checked.

**1.5 Who this is for** — bullets, specific. Roles, life stage, situation, what they've already tried.

**1.6 Who this is not for** — bullets, blunter than feels comfortable. This section does more work than 1.5. It's what makes the right person feel found.

---

## PART II · The Persona

**2.1 The archetype** — who the coach is in this work. Written as a portrait, not a label. What they do, what they refuse to do, what makes them different from the obvious version of the same archetype.

**2.2 What we are / what we are not** — a two-column table of paired adjectives. Each pair should be a near-miss: the thing we are, beside the thing we're often mistaken for. *Mechanical / mystical. Direct / cruel. Warm / soft.* Near-misses calibrate; opposites don't.

**2.3 Operating principles** — four to seven postures, each with a heading and a short paragraph explaining *why* it holds. These are what someone reasons from when the document doesn't cover their situation, so explain the logic rather than just stating the rule.

**2.4 The two hero journeys** — the coach's, against the enemy. The client's, against the same enemy at a different rank. Short. These are the source of every origin story, About page, and podcast answer the coach will ever need.

---

## PART III · Voice

**3.1 The voice principles** — five to seven tests every line of copy passes. Each written as a question, each with an off-brand example and an on-brand example. The examples are the actual content; the principle is just the label.

**3.2–3.4 The registers** — one section per register. For each:

- Where it lives (specific surfaces — not "social media" but "LinkedIn openers, video hooks, Substack headlines")
- How it sounds (bullets)
- Its cadence (the beats it moves through — e.g. *interrupt → mechanism → next move*)
- Four to six sample lines at full strength
- Length conventions where they matter
- What it never does

Brick-and-mortar adds a fourth register: the floor voice.

---

## PART IV · Lexicon

**4.1 The YES list, in three layers.** Keep the layers visibly separate — they have different rules.

- *Layer 1 — Proprietary terms.* Table: term, when to use it. These are the brand's own words; use them with stubborn consistency, because repetition is what turns a coined term into an asset.
- *Layer 2 — Methodology vocabulary, verbatim.* Table: term, what it means, which training it comes from. **These are never renamed or spun.** The fidelity is the credibility line back to the coach's actual qualification, and renaming makes their own training illegible to everyone else in that world. A coach with three modalities has three sub-layers; all three stay intact.
- *Layer 3 — Bridge vocabulary.* Table: term, how we use it. The audience's own language, borrowed so the work lands instantly.

**4.2 The NO list.** Table: banned word or phrase, and one line on why. The reason is what makes the rule survive a contractor who doesn't share the coach's taste.

Include a line about client language: whether banned words stay banned when a client uses them. (Usually yes — mirroring is the most common way a voice erodes.)

If any word looks banned but isn't — because it's load-bearing in the methodology — say so explicitly with the exception spelled out. Ambiguity here produces either sloppy copy or over-correction.

**4.3 Concept glossary.** The brand's proper nouns — named concepts, characters, programs, artifacts. Two to eight, no more. A cast that needs a chart is a cast nobody will remember.

---

## PART V · Persona Hooks

One section per persona. For each:

- **The pain we name** — one line, in their language.
- **The flattery they don't notice** — what we respect about them that we never say directly. This is what makes copy land instead of insult.
- **The provocation** — the uncomfortable true thing only they need to hear.
- **A hero line** — one quotable sentence aimed at exactly this person.
- **Vocabulary that lands** — six to ten words from their world.
- **What they've already bought** — the failed-purchase list, which doubles as the objection map.
- **Buying readiness** — where they sit, and whether this brand is built to capture their attention, their money, or both.

Mark the beachhead persona clearly.

**If personas have not been validated against real interviews, label them UNVALIDATED at the top of Part V.** A coach who forgets which parts are hypotheses will build a year of content on someone who doesn't exist.

---

## PART VI · The Copy Engine

The part that makes the voice reproducible by someone who isn't the coach.

**6.1 Headline formulas** — four to six fill-in-the-blank patterns, each with two or three filled examples. Build them from *this* brand's enemy and archetype so the pattern already carries the position.

**6.2 Hook structures** — three to five opening patterns for the first seconds of anything.

**6.3 CTA patterns** — what the buttons and closers say. Include a short list of CTAs this brand never writes.

**6.4 The manifesto** — 600 to 1,000 words of the voice at full length, no headers, no bullets, the argument made in full.

This is the single most useful artifact in the document. It becomes the calibration reference: when anyone is unsure whether a draft fits, they read it back to back with the manifesto and listen for the difference. It does more to make a voice reproducible than any list of adjectives ever will. Write it in the coach's voice, from their material, and read it back to them before locking it.

---

## PART VII · Visual Identity

Stub at this stage:

> Visual system to be built in a separate session. See the **Production Kit** skill — colors, typography, logo standards, imagery direction, environment, and video grammar, all derived from the archetype and voice established in this document.
>
> Interim rule: [one or two constraints already implied by the archetype — e.g. "no stock photography," "no gradients," "mono type for anything diagnostic"]

Resist building the visual system now. Identity first, production second — visual work done before the voice is settled gets redone, and a coach who spends their energy on a palette before their positioning is sound has been badly served.

---

## PART VIII · The Quality Bar

**8.1 The gut check** — five yes/no questions any piece of copy must pass before it ships. Derived from what *this* brand keeps getting wrong, not from a template. If a coach's drift is toward softness, one question should catch softness.

**8.2 Anti-patterns** — four to six worked examples in this shape:

> **Failure — [name of the failure mode]**
> **Off:** [the near-miss copy]
> **Why:** [the specific axis it failed on]
> **Rewrite:** [the fixed version]

Use the coach's own near-misses. They teach far more than invented bad examples, because the failure is subtle and the coach recognizes their own reflex.

---

## PART IX · [Lens-specific]

- **Transformation brand** → Brand Architecture
- **Personal brand** → The Operator
- **Brick-and-mortar** → Leading This Place

See the relevant lens file for contents.

## PART X · Working Here *(brick-and-mortar only)*

Written for staff, not for the owner. See **Appendix C**.

---

## Colophon

- Brand, operator, document version, date.
- Methodology sources, credited by name. *(If the coach is certified in someone else's method, name the method and its originators. It costs nothing and it's the honest thing.)*
- **Known contradictions** — anything the Contradiction Check surfaced that the coach chose to keep. Written as a decision, not an oversight.
- **Rejected cuts** — the stress-test charges the coach declined, with their reasoning. Useful later, when someone asks why.
- **Version history** — what changed between versions and why. This document is going to move, and the coach needs to see what moved.
- One closing line: the question to ask when in doubt. Usually a compressed restatement of the archetype. *"When in doubt, ask: would [the archetype] do this? If no, rewrite."*

---

## Delivery

Markdown as the source of truth. Offer .docx and .pdf as well — coaches share these with designers, contractors, and staff who won't open a markdown file.

Version it 1.0 and tell the coach plainly: this document changes. The stress test will produce revisions, the field test will reshape the personas, and the first three months of actually using it will teach them more than this session did.


---

# APPENDIX G · Worked Example

The case this kit was reverse-engineered from. A real brand, live, built in about two weeks of AI-assisted sessions.

Read it for calibration — how sharp the output should be, and what each phase actually produces. Show a coach the Phase 1 and Phase 2 outputs when they ask what they're going to end up with; it's more persuasive than any description of the process.

**The brand:** `>beRewritten_` — a 90-day language and nervous-system coaching program for burned-out senior tech operators. Transformation-brand lens. Founder was certified in a language-and-breath coaching methodology and had fifteen years in tech, including his own repeated burnout.

---

## Phase 0 · Intake

Raw material on hand: three levels of certification in one methodology, four recorded beta group sessions, fifteen years in the industry he'd be selling to, and his own history as the exact person he wanted to serve.

The intake finding that mattered most: **he was the former patient.** That's rare and it shortens Phase 3 dramatically. When a coach isn't the former patient, Phase 4 has to work much harder and the field test matters more.

---

## Phase 1 · The Enemy

Where a generic kit would have asked "what's your mission," this asked what the lie in the industry was. What came back was three antagonists, not one — and naming them as a set turned out to be more powerful than a single enemy, because it defined a whole region of the market as hostile territory.

> **The Trauma Industrial Complex** — insists every problem requires five years of archaeology before you're allowed to feel okay.
> **The Wellness Industrial Complex** — sells you breathwork apps for a problem that won't be fixed by shallower breathing.
> **The Productivity Industrial Complex** — whispers that your nervous-system collapse is a calendar issue.

And the mechanism that made it a position rather than a complaint:

> Each of those industries has a vested financial interest in your problem being permanent and complicated. Our entire model assumes the opposite.

**What to notice.** All three have a *business model*, which is what separates a real enemy from a vibe. "Hustle culture" would have failed here — nobody profits from it in a way you can point at. "An industry that bills monthly for a problem it never solves" is falsifiable, specific, and immediately generates copy.

**The inversion that produced it.** The consensus position in this market is *burnout is a wellness problem requiring rest and self-care*. The weak inversion is *burnout is not a wellness problem*. The strong inversion changed the category entirely: **burnout is a mechanical fault in language, and mechanical faults don't need a five-year study — they need a wrench.** That recategorization is the entire brand, and it came from an inversion pass, not from a brainstorm.

---

## Phase 2 · The Archetype

The archetype: **a mechanic.**

Its origin was a line written for an earlier product: *"When your tire falls off on the highway, you don't need a longitudinal study from PhDs to fix it — you need a wrench."*

Then the critical refinement, which took a second pass: a mechanic normally fixes the thing for you, and that would have made the brand another authority selling dependence — the very thing it was against. So the archetype got a constraint:

> This mechanic does not turn the wrench for you. He reads the diagnostic, finds the fault, and hands you the wrench.

That one constraint made the archetype defensible against *both* enemies simultaneously — against the trauma industry (which makes the client a permanent patient) and the productivity industry (which sells a system to follow). It also happened to be a precise description of what the underlying methodology actually is: a questions-based practice, not an advice-based one.

**The extension test, passed:**

| Slot | Answer |
|---|---|
| The product | The 90-Day Rewrite |
| The free thing | The Syntax Diagnostic |
| The CTA verb | Apply · Take the diagnostic |
| Stuck state | A corrupted script |
| Working state | Patched · Compiled · Rewritten |
| The method's name | Syntax Audit → Patch the Code → Install the Defense |
| The diagnostic | The Cognitive Load Audit *(same thing, renamed for engineers)* |

Seven of seven, cleanly. That's what a real archetype looks like: one choice, and the entire naming problem is solved permanently. The logo fell out of it too — a terminal prompt and a blinking cursor.

**Calibration note.** If a coach's archetype can't fill five of these slots without straining, it's decoration. Throw it out and take the next candidate. Do not proceed with a pleasant metaphor that doesn't generate.

---

## Phase 3 · The Expensive Problem and the Transformation

**The expensive problem, in the brand's own words:**

> The burned-out tech operator who has tried everything reasonable and is one Slack ping away from torching the career they spent fifteen years building.

Note what makes it expensive: fifteen years of career capital, quantified elsewhere as *"somewhere between $400K of unvested equity and a career-ending breakdown."* Not "stress." Not "overwhelm." A number and a decade.

**The transformation, made observable:**

> In 90 days, you will know exactly which of your scripts is corrupted, exactly what to say to the people you've been avoiding, and exactly how to make a decision without your nervous system making it for you.

And the anti-promise directly after it: *"Not enlightenment. Not balance."* Naming what you're *not* promising is a credibility move most brands skip, and it costs nothing.

**Calibration note.** The middle clause — *exactly what to say to the people you've been avoiding* — is the observable one. A stranger could verify it. That's the standard to hold coaches to when they offer "feel more confident."

---

## Phase 4 · The People

Four personas, framed as **"four ways the same operating system fails"** rather than as demographics — Hero, Cynic, Hollow, Fawn. Each got a name, a script, a language bank, and a provocation.

The part most brand kits never do, and the reason to insist on it:

**Buying readiness was ranked separately from pain level.**

> Tier 1 — the Fawn and the Hollow buy now. Both have cash and both already consider coaching a category they purchase from.
> Tier 2 — the Hero is the flywheel. Most money, most pain, hardest ego defense. He will not buy "coaching." He will buy *a diagnostic engineering audit on himself.* When he buys, he refers other Heroes.
> Tier 3 — the Cynic consumes content for eighteen months before he buys. Build content for him. Do not bank revenue against him.
>
> **Strategic call: build the voice for the Hero and the Cynic — the voice is the moat. Monetize the Fawn and the Hollow in the meantime.**

That last line is a decision no brand kit would have produced from a persona template. It only appears when you force the two rankings apart.

**The spend pattern as diagnosis** — each persona's failed purchases were sorted by *category of thing bought*:

> The Hero buys **amplifiers**, never brakes. The Cynic buys **escape routes**. The Hollow buys **vibes**. The Fawn buys **systems**.
>
> None of them have paid for syntax. That is the gap I sit in.

Four words — amplifiers, escape routes, vibes, systems — and the entire market gap is visible. Push coaches for this level of compression.

**Objections as diagnosis:**

> Every objection is a syntax error speaking in its own voice. *"I don't have time"* → **I am important because I am needed.** *"Too expensive"* → **I am not worth this investment.** *"I should be able to fix this myself"* → **Asking for help means I'm broken.**
>
> The objection isn't a problem to overcome. It's the syntax error showing up for the diagnostic. The right response isn't to argue. It's to name it back.

---

## Phase 5 · The Voice

**The NO list came from the enemy, and it's the reason the voice is enforceable.** Twenty banned words, each with a reason: *healing journey, holding space, self-care, wellness, authentic self, manifesting, container, lean in, just breathe.* Plus the rule that makes it hold: **banned even when a client says them. Especially then.**

One entry is worth studying because it's the kind of nuance a template never catches. The word *thoughts* looks like it belongs on a banned list in this brand. It doesn't — it's load-bearing in the methodology (*observe your thoughts, think about your thinking*). So the Bible bans exactly one form of it: `"Thoughts?"` as a post closer, with a paragraph explaining why the rest is fair game. Precision like that is what stops a NO list from producing over-corrected copy.

**The YES list, in three layers:** proprietary brand terms (Override, Rewrite, Script, the Competence Trap) · methodology vocabulary kept verbatim from the certification, unrenamed and credited · tech-operator bridge vocabulary (bus factor, single point of failure, latency, root cause, race condition).

The middle layer is the one coaches get wrong. The temptation is to rename a certification's terms so they fit the metaphor. Renaming severs the credibility line back to the training and makes the coach illegible to everyone else in that world.

**Three registers, mapped to funnel stages:** Combative (content — the loudest, and the one everything else follows from), Diagnostic (landing pages and sales — same voice, tools set down), Coaching-Room (in-program — warmer, no audience, still mechanical).

**Voice principles as tests with paired examples** — not adjectives:

> **Did we name the trap, or just describe a feeling?**
> Off: *"You're feeling overwhelmed."*
> On: *"You're catching everyone else's chaos and calling it leadership."*
>
> **Did we hand them a wrench, or just hand them a hug?**
> Off: *"It's okay to feel that way."*
> On: *"Open a doc. Write 'What I am actually pretending not to know.' Go."*

---

## Phase 6 · The Stress Test

Run about a month after the Bible was locked, and it produced **nine hard cuts, all of which were accepted.** Including:

- Differentiation was aesthetic, not categorical
- The marketing voice and the delivery voice didn't match
- Four personas was three too many for a beachhead
- The price needed proof
- Safety and scope exposure was the non-negotiable
- The brand-building itself had become a burnout script — for a founder whose brand is about burnout
- Day-job collision
- Premature automation

That's a lot of damage to a document everybody had been proud of a month earlier. It also produced the decisions that made the business real: one beachhead persona instead of four, a lower founding price, and a written screening-and-referral protocol.

**This is the argument for Phase 6.** Every one of those nine was findable at the time the Bible was written. Nobody looked, because the document was exciting and internally coherent. Coherence is not correctness, and an AI that helped build something will not spontaneously attack it.

---

## Phase 7 · Assembly

A versioned Brand Bible — v2.1.1 by the time it settled, with a changelog documenting every shift and why. Roughly 15,000 words across eight parts, delivered as markdown with .docx and .pdf exports.

It has been handed to AI tools, used to generate a website, a hundred-post content catalog, an application form, and email sequences — all of which came out recognizably in the same voice, months later, without the founder in the loop for each one.

**That is the actual test of a Brand Bible.** Not whether it reads well. Whether someone else — a contractor, a staff member, a model — can be handed it and produce something that sounds right.

---

## The two transferable lessons

**One archetype did all the naming.** Product, diagnostic, phases, CTA verbs, logo, visual system, even the failure states — all generated from a single metaphor choice. If a coach finds themselves inventing each of those separately, the archetype is too weak. Go back to Phase 2 and take another candidate.

**The banned list is what made the voice survive.** Anyone can write one good paragraph in a brand voice. What makes a voice hold up six months later, in the hands of someone else, is a specific list of words that get a draft rejected — and a rule that the list applies even when a client uses those words first.
